title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were invoked because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. This revision removes low‑level provenance text from the main prose and explicitly reconciles runtime determinism: determinism in this run derives from adapter semantics that enforced a single shared initial generation per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200), not from an asserted temperature setting. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle and referenced compactly below for auditability (canonical artifact names).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent→network‑configuration translation with generative language models promises operational efficiency but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair depends jointly on (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompt policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study uses a paired design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, a single automated repair on that identical candidate.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies across LLM applications document factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; proposed mitigations include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, guarded agent architectures, and structured validator toolchains. NetOps prototypes demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration generation but commonly lack instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate evaluations against deterministic validators and independent emulators. Red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show that agentic tool use and tool‑description ambiguity can materially affect safety outcomes. Our study contributes an externally auditable, preregistered, paired measurement isolating the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and inferential plan. The sealed preregistration (study id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1 and multiplicity handling was preregistered (single confirmatory test; secondary analyses exploratory).
sections.results: Execution accounting. The run executed autonomously under the frozen plan and completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200. Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter/provider audit fields record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation = 200. Validator outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate is 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary checks. A preregistered Mininet‑based emulator was applied as a secondary disagreement detector to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the contamination summary reports zero disagreement flags in that holdout. Because no validator failures occurred, the preregistered repair branch was never invoked and secondary estimands (repair iterations, model‑call cost per repair, GVR‑introduced failures) have no empirical data for this run.
sections.discussion: Conditional interpretation. The degenerate paired outcome (no discordant pairs) is an artifact‑grounded empirical result: under the fixed generator/prompt policy and the shared‑initial design, every generated candidate satisfied the primary validator’s checks. This null outcome does not imply that GVR is never useful; rather it precisely indicates that, for the tested workload and generation policy, there were no validator‑detectable failures for repair to reduce. Diagnostic artifacts explain the null: task encodings contained explicit required_sequences and workflow constraints; validator traces report parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and violation_count = 0 for representative tasks; difficulty labels (medium/hard/very_hard) indicate the task bank exercised nontrivial dependency patterns even when outputs were correct. The Mininet holdout (20 tasks) revealed no validator–emulator disagreements in this run, but exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout draw is limited by a reproducibility gap (missing labeled holdout selection seed in the labeled artifacts), which we disclose.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent on this task bank under the chosen generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. The artifact‑grounded outcome underscores that GVR’s marginal value depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage; future confirmatory studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity with larger emulator or device checks, allow multi‑sample generation and multi‑step repair budgets, and evaluate multiple models or ensembles to probe model‑dependent brittleness.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (adapter accounting confirms a single shared invocation per task). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent checks; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
